Oxnard Union High School District

Brand Style Guide

How to use our logo, colors, and type consistently — across print, web, presentations, and AI-generated materials. Everyone creating district materials should reference this page before designing anything new.

Logo Library

Logo files & when to use them

Eight approved variations. Pick the one that matches your background color and layout — never recreate, redraw, or approximate the logo by any other means.

Each card includes vector (SVG) and high-resolution transparent (PNG) downloads.
Spacing

Clear space

Always keep the area immediately around the logo free of text, images, and edges — so it can breathe and stays legible.

Clear space
Clear space
The rule: minimum clear space on every side equals the cap-height of the letters in "OXNARD UNION" (the top line of the wordmark) — shown as the dashed box above, measured from this brand file. Nothing else — text, photos, other logos, the edge of the page — may enter that zone. When the logo is resized, the clear space scales with it proportionally.
Protecting the mark

How not to alter the logo

The logo's proportions, colors, and construction are fixed. If you find yourself dragging a corner handle, changing a fill color, or adding an effect — stop.

Usability

Using color accessibly on screen

"Web-safe colors" used to mean the 216-color palette built for 1990s monitors that could only show 256 colors — every modern screen has moved past that, so it's not a real constraint anymore. What still matters is contrast: whether text is actually legible against its background. That's what this section pairs our palette against.

ℹ️ WCAG accessibility guidelines require at least 4.5:1 contrast for normal body text, and at least 3:1 for large text (18px+, or 14px+ bold) and UI elements like icons, buttons, and input borders. The table below checks every palette color against both white and dark (ink) text so you don't have to guess.
ColorWhite textDark textRecommended use

Don't mix Red text on Blue (or Blue on Red)

Oxnard Red directly on Oxnard Blue measures about 2.15:1 — well under the 3:1 minimum for even large text. Always separate them with white, black, or plenty of neutral space instead of layering one directly on the other.

Buttons & CTAs

Use the Base or Shade 20%/40% colors as button backgrounds with white text — both colors pass AAA there. Avoid light tints behind white text; they don't have enough contrast to meet even the minimum.

Light tints are for fills, not white text

Blue Tint 60%/80% and the red tints are great as subtle background fills, chips, or hover states with dark ink text on top — not as a background for white text, which fails contrast there.

Links & interactive text

Oxnard Blue on a white background passes AAA and reads clearly as a link. Underline links regardless of color — color alone shouldn't be the only signal something is clickable.

Fonts

Two typefaces, one job each. Don't substitute system fonts (Arial, Calibri, Helvetica) when these are available.

Tagline

Our tagline — use it deliberately

The current tagline reinforces the district's mission when the full lockup appears in formal contexts. But unlike the logo, the tagline is not permanent — treat it accordingly.

!

The tagline changes over time — the logo doesn't

The tagline reflects the district's current goals and priorities, and it's revisited periodically — it hasn't stayed the same for long historically. Anything printed, built, or published with today's wording risks looking dated once it's updated. Before adding the tagline to anything, ask: "Will this still be in use after the wording changes?" If the answer is yes, or you're not sure, leave the tagline off and use the logo on its own — it's the version that never goes out of date.

When to use it, and when to leave it off
✓ Good fit for the tagline
  • Awards, honors, and recognitions — framed or archived once, as-is
  • Signage or programs for a single dated event (a specific graduation, gala, fundraiser)
  • Anything that already carries the current year (annual report cover, dated press release)
  • The district's annual welcome letter or message templates, reviewed and refreshed yearly
  • Time-boxed campaigns or initiatives with a defined end date
✕ Leave the tagline off
  • Building signage, monuments, engraved plaques, vehicle decals
  • Uniforms, spirit wear, or any physical goods meant to last for years
  • Website headers/footers, favicons, or other evergreen digital touchpoints
  • Standard letterhead, business cards, or templates reused indefinitely across staff turnover
  • Handbooks, policy documents, or anything else with a multi-year shelf life
Rule of thumb: if a piece can't confidently be replaced or reviewed the next time the tagline is updated, default to the logo without the tagline. Before publishing anything that does include it, confirm with the communications team that the wording shown above is still current — the goal is to never have a policy, sign, or template still showing an outdated tagline.
✓ Do
Use the exact wording, capitalization, and punctuation shown above, every time it appears.
✓ Do
Use it only as part of the official lockup asset (the SVG/PNG from the Logo section) — never retype it in a different font or color combination.
Working with AI

Using the logo when prompting AI for flyers

Image generators can't reproduce this logo exactly — every attempt invents a new, slightly-wrong variation (different proportions, a redrawn bird, shifted colors). Never ask an AI tool to draw, generate, recreate, or include the district logo. Instead, treat the logo as a fixed asset you place on top of AI-generated artwork.

1

Generate artwork only

Prompt the AI tool for background imagery, illustration, or photography only — no logos, no text, no seals or emblems.

2

Leave clear space

Ask for negative space in a corner or edge (e.g. "empty space in the top-left") sized for the logo plus its clear space.

3

Place the real logo

Drop in the official PNG/SVG from this page in Canva, Photoshop, Illustrator, or Google Slides — never let the AI tool render it.

4

Add real text

Set headlines in Montserrat and body copy in Open Sans by hand — AI-rendered text is frequently misspelled or off-font.

✕ Avoid "Create a flyer for Oxnard Union High School District with their logo, tagline, and school colors announcing back-to-school night."
✓ Use instead "Generate a bright, photographic background of a high school campus at golden hour, wide open sky, empty negative space in the upper third, color palette leaning navy blue and white, no text, no logos, no icons, no seals."

Reference exact hex codes

When asking AI for color guidance elsewhere in a design, use the real values — "#E20031" and "#0033A1" — rather than "school red" or "navy blue," which the model will interpret loosely.

Never re-upload the logo to a generator

Uploading the logo as a reference image and asking an AI tool to "match this style" or "make a version of this" still produces an unofficial variation — even image-to-image tools redraw edges and proportions.

Check clear space before publishing

Once the real logo is placed on the AI-generated background, confirm nothing — text, photo elements, other graphics — sits inside its clear space zone (see the Clear Space section above).

When in doubt, ask

If a project needs a logo treatment not covered on this page (animated, embroidered, die-cut, etc.), request it from the design/communications team rather than approximating it with AI.
